questions.q: The common difference of an A.P. in which $a_{15} - a_{11} = 48$ is:
questions.solution:
Write both terms with the standard formula $a_n = a + (n-1)d$:

$a_{15} = a + 14d$ and $a_{11} = a + 10d$

Subtract — the first term $a$ cancels:

$a_{15} - a_{11} = (a + 14d) - (a + 10d) = 4d$

So $4d = 48$ and $d = \mathbf{12}$.

There is a shortcut worth remembering: **the gap between the 15th and the 11th term is four steps**, and each step is $d$. In general $a_m - a_n = (m - n)d$ — you never need $a$ at all.

Think of a staircase. To know the height of one step you do not need to know how high the ground floor is; you only need the rise between two named steps and how many steps apart they are.

questions.topic: Which term is a given value
questions.q: Which term of the A.P. $-29,\ -26,\ -23,\ \ldots,\ 61$ is $16$?
questions.solution:
First read off $a$ and $d$:

$a = -29$, $d = -26 - (-29) = 3$

Set the $n$th term equal to 16:

$a + (n-1)d = 16$

$-29 + (n-1)3 = 16$

$(n-1)3 = 45$

$n - 1 = 15 \Rightarrow n = 16$

So $16$ is the **16th** term.

(The $61$ at the end just tells you where the A.P. stops; it plays no part in this question.)

A neat check: from $-29$ to $16$ is a climb of $45$, and each step is $3$, so it takes $15$ steps — and after 15 steps from the *first* term you are standing on the 16th.

questions.q: Three numbers in A.P. have the sum $30$. What is its middle term?
questions.solution:
Name the three terms cleverly: $a - d$, $a$, $a + d$ — putting the middle one at the centre.

Now add them:

$(a - d) + a + (a + d) = 3a$

The $-d$ and $+d$ cancel, so the sum is just three times the middle term:

$3a = 30 \Rightarrow a = \mathbf{10}$

Notice you never learn $d$, and you do not need to — there are infinitely many such triples ($9, 10, 11$; $5, 10, 15$; $-20, 10, 40$ …) and every one of them has middle term 10.

The picture is a see-saw. The outer two terms sit the same distance either side of the middle one, so the middle term is exactly the average — the balance point.

questions.q: The next (4th) term of the A.P. $\sqrt{18},\ \sqrt{50},\ \sqrt{98},\ \ldots$ is:
questions.solution:
Those surds do not look like an A.P. until you simplify them:

$\sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}$,  $\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}$,  $\sqrt{98} = 7\sqrt{2}$

Now it is obvious: the multipliers are $3, 5, 7$ — an A.P. with $d = 2\sqrt{2}$. The next multiplier is $9$:

next term $= 9\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{81 \times 2} = \mathbf{\sqrt{162}}$

The trap is adding the numbers *under* the roots. The gaps there are $32$ and $48$ — not equal — so $\sqrt{98} + 32$ would be nonsense.

Pull the perfect square out of each root first, and a disguised A.P. shows its true shape.

questions.q: The number of terms in the A.P. $3,\ 6,\ 9,\ 12,\ \ldots,\ 111$ is:
questions.solution:
Here $a = 3$, $d = 3$, and the last term is $111$.

$a + (n-1)d = 111$

$3 + (n-1)3 = 111$

$(n-1)3 = 108$

$n - 1 = 36 \Rightarrow n = \mathbf{37}$

The tempting wrong answer is $36$, which is $111 \div 3$ — the number of *steps*, not the number of terms.

Think of fence posts and gaps. A fence with 36 gaps has 37 posts, because the first post came before any gap did. Counting terms in an A.P. is the same off-by-one every time.

questions.topic: First term from the sum formula
questions.q: If the sum of the first $n$ terms of an A.P. is $3n^{2} + 4n$ and its common difference is $6$, then its first term is:
questions.solution:
The sum of the first **one** term *is* the first term. So put $n = 1$ into the formula:

$S_1 = 3(1)^{2} + 4(1) = 3 + 4 = \mathbf{7}$

That is the whole question.

Check it against the given common difference: $S_2 = 3(4) + 4(2) = 20$, so the second term is $S_2 - S_1 = 20 - 7 = 13$, and $13 - 7 = 6$ ✓ — exactly the $d$ the question states.

$S_n$ is a running total. Every individual term can be recovered by taking one total away from the next: $a_n = S_n - S_{n-1}$. The first term is simply the case where there is nothing to subtract.

questions.topic: Finding an unknown in three A.P. terms
questions.q: If the first three terms of an A.P. are $3p - 1$, $3p + 5$ and $5p + 1$ respectively, then the value of $p$ is:
questions.solution:
In an A.P. the gap between consecutive terms is always the same, so

$(\text{2nd}) - (\text{1st}) = (\text{3rd}) - (\text{2nd})$

$(3p + 5) - (3p - 1) = (5p + 1) - (3p + 5)$

$6 = 2p - 4$

$2p = 10 \Rightarrow p = \mathbf{5}$

Check: with $p = 5$ the terms are $14$, $20$, $26$ — a common difference of 6 ✓

An equivalent way to say it: the middle term is the average of its neighbours, $2 \times (3p+5) = (3p-1) + (5p+1)$. Same equation, same answer — use whichever you find easier to write down without slipping a sign.

questions.q: The common difference of an A.P. in which $a_{20} - a_{15} = 20$ is:
questions.solution:
The 20th term is five steps beyond the 15th, so

$a_{20} - a_{15} = 5d$

$5d = 20 \Rightarrow d = \mathbf{4}$

Options (C) and (D) are there to catch a half-finished answer: $5d$ is the *expression* for the difference, not the value of $d$. The question asks for the common difference itself, which is a number.

Read the last line of a question again before choosing. Getting to $5d = 20$ is most of the work, and it is a shame to stop one division short.

questions.topic: Reading an A.P. from its nth term
questions.q: If the $n$th term of an A.P. is $a_n = 5n - 3$, then its common difference is:
questions.solution:
Write out the first few terms:

$a_1 = 5(1) - 3 = 2$,  $a_2 = 5(2) - 3 = 7$,  $a_3 = 5(3) - 3 = 12$

The gaps are $7 - 2 = 5$ and $12 - 7 = 5$, so $d = \mathbf{5}$.

More directly:

$a_n - a_{n-1} = (5n - 3) - \big(5(n-1) - 3\big) = 5$

Whenever the $n$th term is a straight line in $n$ — anything of the form $pn + q$ — the **coefficient of $n$ is the common difference** and $p + q$ is the first term. Here $d = 5$ and $a_1 = 5 - 3 = 2$.

That is no accident: an A.P. climbs by the same amount each step, which is exactly what a straight line does.

questions.q: If the sum of the first $m$ terms of an A.P. is the same as the sum of its first $n$ terms $(m \neq n)$, then show that the sum of its first $(m + n)$ terms is zero.
questions.solution:
**Set the two sums equal.** With $S_k = \dfrac{k}{2}\big[2a + (k-1)d\big]$:

$\dfrac{m}{2}\big[2a + (m-1)d\big] = \dfrac{n}{2}\big[2a + (n-1)d\big]$

Multiply by 2 and expand:

$2am + m(m-1)d = 2an + n(n-1)d$

**Gather like terms:**

$2a(m - n) + d\big[m(m-1) - n(n-1)\big] = 0$

$m(m-1) - n(n-1) = m^{2} - m - n^{2} + n = (m^{2} - n^{2}) - (m - n) = (m-n)(m+n) - (m-n) = (m-n)(m+n-1)$

So

$(m - n)\big[2a + (m + n - 1)d\big] = 0$

**Use $m \neq n$.** Since $m - n \neq 0$, the other bracket must vanish:

$2a + (m + n - 1)d = 0$

**Now the sum of $(m+n)$ terms:**

$S_{m+n} = \dfrac{m+n}{2}\big[2a + (m+n-1)d\big] = \dfrac{m+n}{2} \times 0 = \mathbf{0}$ ∎

The condition $m \neq n$ is what makes the whole proof work — it is the licence to divide out $(m-n)$.

What is going on underneath: if two different running totals are equal, everything added in between must have cancelled out, so the A.P. crosses from positive to negative — and it turns out to do so exactly symmetrically.

questions.topic: Three terms from a sum and a sum of squares
questions.q: In an A.P., the sum of three consecutive terms is $24$ and the sum of their squares is $194$. Find the numbers.
questions.solution:
**Choose the names well.** Let the three terms be $a - d$, $a$, $a + d$.

**First condition:**

$(a - d) + a + (a + d) = 24 \Rightarrow 3a = 24 \Rightarrow a = 8$

**Second condition:**

$(a - d)^{2} + a^{2} + (a + d)^{2} = 194$

Expand: $(a^{2} - 2ad + d^{2}) + a^{2} + (a^{2} + 2ad + d^{2}) = 3a^{2} + 2d^{2}$

The $2ad$ terms cancel, leaving

$3(8)^{2} + 2d^{2} = 194$

$192 + 2d^{2} = 194 \Rightarrow d^{2} = 1 \Rightarrow d = \pm 1$

**The numbers** are $7, 8, 9$ (or $9, 8, 7$ if you take $d = -1$ — the same three numbers, read backwards).

**Check:** $7 + 8 + 9 = 24$ ✓ and $49 + 64 + 81 = 194$ ✓

The reason for writing the terms as $a-d, a, a+d$ rather than $a, a+d, a+2d$ is that it makes the middle term the centre of symmetry — so the awkward cross terms cancel themselves in both conditions, and two messy equations become two easy ones.

questions.topic: Sum of n terms from two given sums
questions.q: If the sum of the first 7 terms of an A.P. is $49$ and that of the first 17 terms is $289$, find the sum of its first 20 terms.
questions.solution:
**Write both conditions** using $S_k = \dfrac{k}{2}\big[2a + (k-1)d\big]$.

$S_7 = \dfrac{7}{2}\big[2a + 6d\big] = 7(a + 3d) = 49 \Rightarrow a + 3d = 7$ … (1)

$S_{17} = \dfrac{17}{2}\big[2a + 16d\big] = 17(a + 8d) = 289 \Rightarrow a + 8d = 17$ … (2)

**Subtract (1) from (2):**

$5d = 10 \Rightarrow d = 2$, and then $a = 7 - 6 = 1$.

**Now the 20-term sum:**

$S_{20} = \dfrac{20}{2}\big[2(1) + 19(2)\big] = 10\big[2 + 38\big] = 10 \times 40 = \mathbf{400}$

**Check:** $S_7 = \tfrac{7}{2}(2 + 12) = 49$ ✓ and $S_{17} = \tfrac{17}{2}(2 + 32) = 289$ ✓

There is a pattern hiding here: $49 = 7^{2}$, $289 = 17^{2}$ and $400 = 20^{2}$. With $a = 1$ and $d = 2$ this is the A.P. of odd numbers $1, 3, 5, 7, \ldots$, and the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers is always $n^{2}$ — a fact worth carrying into the exam hall.

questions.topic: First term and common difference from a ratio
questions.q: The ratio of the 10th term to the 30th term of an A.P. is $1 : 3$ and the sum of its first six terms is $42$. Find the first term and the common difference of the A.P.
questions.solution:
**Turn the ratio into an equation.**

$\dfrac{a_{10}}{a_{30}} = \dfrac{a + 9d}{a + 29d} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Cross-multiply:

$3(a + 9d) = a + 29d$

$3a + 27d = a + 29d$

$2a = 2d \Rightarrow a = d$

**Use the sum.**

$S_6 = \dfrac{6}{2}\big[2a + 5d\big] = 3(2a + 5d) = 42 \Rightarrow 2a + 5d = 14$

Substitute $d = a$:

$2a + 5a = 14 \Rightarrow 7a = 14 \Rightarrow a = 2$, and so $d = 2$.

The first term is **2** and the common difference is **2**.

**Check:** $a_{10} = 2 + 18 = 20$, $a_{30} = 2 + 58 = 60$, and $20 : 60 = 1 : 3$ ✓ The first six terms are $2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12$, summing to $42$ ✓

Two facts, two unknowns. The ratio alone cannot pin down $a$ and $d$ — it only fixes their *relationship* ($a = d$) — and the sum is what fixes the scale.

questions.q: If the sum of the first 14 terms of an A.P. is $1050$ and its first term is $10$, then find the 20th term and the $n$th term.
questions.solution:
**Use the sum to find $d$.**

$S_{14} = \dfrac{14}{2}\big[2a + 13d\big] = 7\big[2(10) + 13d\big] = 1050$

$20 + 13d = 150$

$13d = 130 \Rightarrow d = 10$

**The 20th term:**

$a_{20} = a + 19d = 10 + 19(10) = \mathbf{200}$

**The $n$th term:**

$a_n = a + (n-1)d = 10 + (n-1)10 = \mathbf{10n}$

**Check:** the A.P. is $10, 20, 30, \ldots$ Its first 14 terms sum to $10(1 + 2 + \cdots + 14) = 10 \times 105 = 1050$ ✓ and $a_{20} = 200$ ✓

Once $a_n$ came out as the clean $10n$, the A.P. revealed itself as simply the multiples of ten. Always simplify the $n$th term at the end — a tidy form is both easier to check and a sign you have not slipped.

questions.topic: Number of terms and common difference
questions.q: The first term of an A.P. is $5$, the last term is $45$ and the sum of all the terms is $400$. Find the number of terms and the common difference of the A.P.
questions.solution:
**When the last term is known**, use the other sum formula:

$S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + l)$, where $l$ is the last term.

$400 = \dfrac{n}{2}(5 + 45) = \dfrac{n}{2}(50) = 25n$

$n = \mathbf{16}$

**Now the common difference**, from the last term being the 16th:

$a + (n-1)d = l$

$5 + 15d = 45$

$15d = 40 \Rightarrow d = \dfrac{40}{15} = \mathbf{\dfrac{8}{3}}$

**Check:** $S_{16} = \dfrac{16}{2}(5 + 45) = 8 \times 50 = 400$ ✓

Picking the right formula saves the whole question. $S_n = \tfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$ needs no $d$ at all, so it hands you $n$ immediately; the other version, $\tfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$, would have left you with two unknowns tangled together.

Why it works: pair the first term with the last, the second with the second-to-last, and so on. Every pair adds to the same total $a + l$, and there are $\tfrac{n}{2}$ pairs.
